items.content:
US Stock Futures Rise Ahead of Technology Earnings as Oil Prices Decline: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Trading floor of the New York stock exchange ©Carol M. Highsmith Archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division US stock futures moved higher on Monday as investors prepared for quarterly earnings from major technology companies amid concerns about artificial intelligence investment and financing conditions. Oil prices declined following US President Donald Trump's decision to waive certain sanctions on Russia, while Chinese economic data showed an acceleration in third-quarter growth.
Futures linked to the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 advanced in early trading, following declines in the main Wall Street indices on Friday.
Investors were also assessing preliminary financial results from Chinese memory chip manufacturer ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), whose shares declined despite forecasts of substantial revenue growth and a return to profitability.
US Futures Advance Following Technology Sector Declines
At 03:06 ET (07:06 GMT), Dow Jones futures had risen 215 points, or 0.4%, while S&P 500 futures gained 53 points, or 0.7%.
Nasdaq 100 futures increased 384 points, equivalent to 1.3%.
The gains followed a decline in US equities on Friday, when concerns about financing requirements and valuations across the artificial intelligence sector affected technology stocks.
Analysts at Vital Knowledge described investor sentiment towards AI-related equities as "considerably darker".
The firm highlighted concerns about the sustainability of debt and equity issuance used to finance the expansion of AI infrastructure.
Media reports indicating that quarterly revenue growth at Anthropic, the developer of the Claude AI model, remained substantial but had slowed compared with the preceding quarter also contributed to investor attention on the sector.
Vital Knowledge analysts said: "While many stocks are still above their summer lows, the psychology towards the group seems worse than it was in June and July, due in large part to the dramatic worsening in certain pockets of the AI credit market."
Analysts at ING also examined the potential implications of technology market volatility for the US dollar.
The bank said the dollar "could be a laggard in further stock market instability", although it did not anticipate an imminent substantial decline in the currency.
The assessment reflects concerns that changes in investor positioning towards AI-related assets could affect other financial markets.
Investors are continuing to evaluate the financing requirements of major technology companies and the potential relationship between infrastructure expenditure, revenue growth and future profitability.
Quarterly earnings from major US technology companies will be a focus during the week, particularly as investors assess spending on artificial intelligence.
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is scheduled to report its results after the US market close on Wednesday.
The company has expanded its AI activities following the September launch of its Muse model, which reportedly attracted millions of downloads.
The technology includes services designed to assist users with travel bookings and small-business tasks.
Meta has also released an open-weight version of its Muse Spark model for coding applications.
Investors will be examining Meta's financial performance and management commentary on AI investment, capital expenditure and the commercial development of its technology.
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) is also scheduled to publish quarterly results after Wednesday's closing bell.
The company recently attracted attention following a live demonstration in which a booster-powered vehicle completed a controlled landing.
Both earnings announcements come during a period of increased scrutiny of technology companies' investment programmes and growth expectations.
Oil Prices Fall Following US Decision on Russian Sanctions
Crude oil prices declined on Monday after President Donald Trump issued an executive order suspending numerous sanctions on Russia shortly before their scheduled implementation.
The administration also waived proposed tariffs on countries importing Russian oil.
At 03:56 ET, Brent crude futures fell 2.6% to $106.97 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures declined 2.0% to $99.36 per barrel.
The declines followed a gain of nearly 5% in crude prices during the previous week, when concerns about supply disruptions, particularly in the Middle East, supported the market.
The US measures raised expectations that additional Russian crude could remain available to international buyers.
Trump subsequently indicated on social media that maintaining Russia's participation in negotiations was among the considerations behind his approach to efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
Earlier, the president had said that no final decision had been made, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the administration could take up to 60 days to assess the economic effects of the waivers.
Chinese memory chip manufacturer ChangXin Memory Technologies forecast a substantial increase in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, citing demand associated with artificial intelligence and higher memory chip prices.
In a preliminary earnings estimate, CXMT projected revenue of between 265 billion yuan and 270 billion yuan, equivalent to approximately $39.6 billion to $40.4 billion.
The forecast compares with revenue of 32.08 billion yuan in the corresponding period of 2025, representing an increase of more than eight times.
The company also expects net profit attributable to shareholders of between 131 billion yuan and 132.5 billion yuan.
This would represent a reversal from the net loss of 5.28 billion yuan recorded in the first nine months of the previous year.
Despite the projected improvement in financial performance, CXMT shares declined.
The share price movement came amid heightened investor expectations for companies benefiting from demand for AI-related semiconductor products.
China's Third-Quarter GDP Growth Accelerates to 4.5%
China's economy expanded faster than expected in the third quarter of 2026, supported by exports and demand associated with artificial intelligence.
Data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed gross domestic product increased 4.5% year on year in the three months ended September 30.
The result exceeded economists' expectations for 4.4% growth and represented an acceleration from the 4.3% annual increase recorded in the preceding quarter.
On a quarter-on-quarter basis, GDP grew 1.2%, compared with forecasts of 1.1% and growth of 0.9% in the second quarter.
For the first nine months of 2026, China's economy expanded by 4.6%.
The figures place growth within the government's previously stated annual target range of 4.5% to 5%.
Investors Monitor Earnings, Energy Markets and Chinese Growth
Financial markets began the week with gains in US stock futures, lower crude oil prices and further developments in the technology sector.
The upcoming earnings announcements from Meta and Tesla will provide additional information about corporate performance and investment plans.
At the same time, changes to US sanctions on Russia are influencing expectations for global oil supply, while China's economic data and CXMT's preliminary results provide further indications of activity in the Chinese economy and semiconductor industry.

items.title: Australian Greens senator denies claims of misconduct towards women
items.summary: Jordon Steele-John says the timing of the claims is motivated by "nasty political games" within the Greens.
items.content:
Image caption, Greens senator Jordon Steele-John denies claims of misconduct against women
An Australian Greens senator has denied allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women and accused his party of "nasty political games", days after the claims emerged.
Last Thursday, Greens leader David Shoebridge said Senator Jordon Steele-John, 32, had taken leave from the party room after a letter from seven current and former members said he had been accused of "multiple allegations" of misconduct between 2017 and 2025.
In an online post on Sunday, the senator denied the claims and said he was not on leave. On a sexual assault claim, he said police investigating the matter had closed the case and no charges were laid.
An internal party probe has been launched into the allegations.
Steele-John, who has cerebral palsy and uses a wheelchair, was first elected to the senate in Western Australia in November 2017.
In his letter responding to the claims, Steele-John said his nickname - "Feels on wheels" - initially referred to him being emotional when advocating for disability rights but had since taken on a "more sinister meaning" about his alleged mistreatment of women.
He accused Shoebridge of mishandling the matter and questioned the timing of the letter, saying "it is no coincidence" that the allegations were sent to the leader "the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection" ahead of the next federal election.
Days after the letter with the claims was sent to Shoebridge, local media reported that the party had created a 47-page dossier years earlier that listed a number of allegations against Steele-John and how to manage media coverage if they emerged.
Steele-John said the dossier was made so that the media would not "bombard" the two women at the centre of those claims and that neither woman had made a complaint.
He acknowledged the allegations against him would have "damaged" the public's trust in him and said he was "committed to rebuilding that by acting with as much transparency and accountability as I can".
Shoebridge's office confirmed that the allegations had been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.
A spokesperson for Shoebridge said the leader still believed "leave is appropriate under the circumstances" and taking leave would not influence the internal party investigation.

items.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
items.summary: Two men tell of the work they say they have been doing to support Ukrainian intelligence during the war.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Russian saboteur working for Ukraine shares reconnaissance videos
Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.
One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.
He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.
Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.
He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow , Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.
Image caption, Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was killed in Moscow last year by an explosive device hidden under his car
There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.
The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."
And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.
The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.
There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.
It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.
If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube , external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine
Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.
"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the warâ¦ Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.
His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.
"When these [drone] components are combinedâ¦ it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.
He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.
If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.
Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.
Image caption, Foma explained how he taught his undercover volunteers to trail Russian officers
"You will get a file... from me or a colleagueâ¦ with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.
Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.
He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.
"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals liveâ¦ Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.
"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."
He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.
Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.
"As a ruleâ¦ we also check the data [on that person]â¦ Only after that we say whether we work or not."
But he argued that his team's actions were justified.
"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraineâ¦ to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."
Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.
Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."
But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.
Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.
After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year , external . One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.
Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.
"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.
To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.
"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chatsâ¦ leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.
Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.
"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.
Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.
Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.
So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.
Image caption, Marcin waiting to meet Ivan in Georgia - we were surprised by Ivan's apparent freedom to travel
Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.
"You go to a third countryâ¦ where [Ukraine's] agents meet youâ¦ and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.
Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".
But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.
Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.
"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holesâ¦ and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.
Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.
"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."
But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.

items.summary: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"  CBS News<a href="https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitwFBVV
items.content:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is due in Tehran on Monday for his first visit since the U.S. launched its war with Iran almost eight months ago . He said he will hold talks "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war" in the region.
Iran's foreign minister said Sunday that Tehran's proposal for a seven-day ceasefire with the U.S. and a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz — if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and sanctions against Iran — remains on the table after being rejected by President Trump last month.
Last week saw 10 attacks on commercial vessels in and near the Strait of Hormuz, according to the U.K. navy, which said October has become the worst month for attacks on shipping in the strait since the early days of the war in March. items.title: Musk and Anthropic pledge public share giveaways
items.summary: Musk's announcement comes after Anthropic pledged to create a public benefit fund ahead of its blockbuster stock market listing.
items.content:
By Peter Hoskins Â  and Â  Michael Race ,Â  Business reporters
Elon Musk's SpaceX and artificial intelligence giant Anthropic have pledged big financial giveaways as Big Tech firms come under pressure over the potential impact of AI on humanity.
Musk said on Monday that he would give one of his shares at his rocket company, which owns xAI, to every child in America next year.
The billionaire's announcement came after Anthropic said it would commit 5% of its shares to a fund that will make donations for the "public good".
Anthropic is laying the ground for a potential blockbuster stock market listing that could value the firm at more than $1tn (Â£750bn). SpaceX set the record for biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history in June, raising $85.7bn.
The pledges come at a time when the AI industry is under intense scrutiny over safety concerns and fears about its impact on society and jobs.
Details over how each American child would be handed a share in SpaceX have not been disclosed.
In a post on social media, , external Musk said: "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many."
It came after he responded to Anthropic's public fund pledge with: "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public. This is what I will be doing."
Anthropic said none of the shares held in its Public Benefit Fund would be used for lobbying or political donations in the US or overseas.
The Claude developer said on Sunday that the fund could also receive another 2% of the firm's shares at its board's discretion.
Last week, Anthropic told prospective investors that its revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (Â£12.6bn) in the three months to the end of September.
In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on developing the technology and building infrastructure to power its models.
Companies around the world, primarily technology firms, have cut thousands of jobs after investing in AI, with many pointing to higher efficiencies from its adoption.
Research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) published in 2024 suggested that almost 40% of jobs around the world will be affected by AI , with that figure rising as high as â60% in advanced economies.
In September, a researcher who quit Anthropic said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.
"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.
Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry.
The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, had previously called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.
The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Musk, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.
Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document , making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.
Trump has repeatedly rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.
Since then, the president has named the director of national intelligence Jay Clayton as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will co-ordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations".

Ukraine bombing oil facilities in Russia and more tankers coming under attack in the Persian Gulf have clouded the supply outlook.
Fires broke out at an oil terminal and depot in St. Petersburg after Ukraine launched a massive wave of drone strikes on Sunday, St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said in a post on Telegram.
The terminal in St. Petersburg exports about 120,000 barrels per day of refined products, mostly fuel oil, according to data from Kpler. It is unclear how bad the damage is at the facility.

In the Middle East, meanwhile, two tankers were attacked off the coast of Saudi Arabia in the Persian Gulf on Friday, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
A small boat fired a rocket-propelled grenade at an unidentified tanker 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubayl, according to UKMTO. Another tanker, the ST3, was hit by an unknown projectile, UKMTO reported.

items.title: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection
items.summary: Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
items.content:
Trump endorses embattled Israeli PM Netanyahu for reelection Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection
FILE - President Donald Trump listens as Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, Dec. 29, 2025, in Palm Beach, Fla.
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump's popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders' strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Elections in Israel will be a verdict on Netanyahu's handling of October 7
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
"Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together," Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. "Together we will complete the mission!"
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump's ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries' key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
Trump confirms calling Netanyahu 'crazy,' says they still get along
In his post, Trump again threatened to "soon finish the job" against Iran "unless they change their ways, rapidly," but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been "Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself."
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump's comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, "I'm not involved in politics anymore," despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.
Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.
Netanyahu rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan, demands Hamas disarm first
Trump criticized Israel's decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu "crazy." Trump also said that he was "a little bit perturbed" as Israel's fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.
Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump's latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the U.S. administration's call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.

S&P 500, Nasdaq set to open higher as AI stocks rebound ahead of earnings rush
Oct 19 (Reuters) - The S&P 500 and Nasdaq indexes were set to open higher on Monday, as AI-related stocks rebounded from last week's sharp selloff, while a decline in oil ‌prices provided additional support ahead of key earnings reports this week.
Both indexes posted their biggest weekly drop since ‌late June on Friday, as concerns that higher interest rates could curb investments in AI infrastructure weighed on technology stocks, particularly data center operators.
The selloff reflected ​mounting investor unease over how the costly AI buildout will be financed, a question that has increasingly pressured companies underpinning the US bull market, which recently marked its fourth anniversary.
AI-linked stocks such as CoreWeave, which had plunged more than 25% last week, climbed 6.6% in premarket trading on Monday. Chipmakers Broadcom and Micron gained more than 3% each.
Megacap stocks were largely up, with Nvidia and ‌Amazon rising more than 2% each. Meta ⁠was up marginally.
Focus is now shifting to a busy week of corporate earnings, with Meta expected to beat Wall Street expectations on Wednesday. Elon Musk-led Tesla's results are also due that day, while ⁠SpaceX is scheduled to report on Tuesday.
Netflix, General Motors and GE Aerospace are also among the companies reporting results this week.
"The tech sell off last week because of the rise in interest rates and the problems with CoreWeave sending shockwaves through the market. I don't ​think ​that is over just yet," said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at ​CFRA Research.
"Certainly, corporate reports are all going to ‌be important this week, but investors will be evaluating which companies are most vulnerable."
The AI boom, increasingly acknowledged by the Federal Reserve as a contributor to inflation, has also complicated policymakers' efforts to rein in price pressures while sustaining broader economic growth amid heavy spending by companies such as Amazon, Apple and Anthropic.
The Fed is expected to keep rates steady at 3.75%-4.00% when it meets on October 27-28, according to LSEG data.
At 08:44 a.m. ET, Dow E-minis were down 125 points, or 0.24%, S&P 500 ‌E-minis were up 34.5 points, or 0.45%, and Nasdaq 100 E-minis were ​up 365.5 points, or 1.24%.
Brent futures were last down 1.5% at around $108.29 ​a barrel, following US President Donald Trump's decision to ​waive some sanctions on Russia. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday the president ‌would take up to 60 days to assess the ​economic impact of such a ​move. [O/R]
Meanwhile, Iran reported another tanker had hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, while the cost of shipping and insurance was keeping oil prices for actual delivery a lot higher.
Intel shares rose 4.2% after J.P.Morgan upgraded the ​stock to "neutral" from "underweight."
Cleveland-Cliffs surged 13.7% after the ‌steelmaker surpassed analysts' estimate for third-quarter profit.
Bitcoin rose 2%, putting it on track for its biggest one-day gain ​in nearly a month. The move lifted crypto-related stocks, with Coinbase up 1.7% and Strategy gaining 2.2%.

A Repeat Of ‘Black Monday' Would Send The S&P 500 Down More Than 1,500 Points And Wipe Out More Than $13 Trillion In Stock Market Value
Thirty-nine years after a single October Monday vaporized trillions and paralyzed markets worldwide, analysts are drawing uncomfortable parallels between 1987 and today's AI-fueled rally, and the math behind a repeat scenario is sobering.
A dramatic red, burning trend line on a financial chart symbolizes a steep market decline, reflecting the volatility and potential for significant losses discussed in relation to events like 'Black Monday'. © Travis Wolfe / Shutterstock.com
The benchmark S&P 500 is still up 11.9% this year, but Wall Street marks Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, the 39th anniversary of the 1987 crash , after a rough week.
On that day in 1987, the Dow Jones Industrial Average suffered its largest one-day percentage drop ever, a 22.6% collapse. But applying Black Monday ‘s 20.47% S&P 500 decline to Friday's close would erase about 1,568 points by our arithmetic, leaving the index near 6,092. The Dow's 22.61% drop would remove about 11,750 points, leaving it near 40,245.
This is simple arithmetic on Friday's closes and is not meant as a prediction.
In dollars, the same S&P 500 decline applied to the index's $68.45 trillion market cap at the end of the third quarter, equals about $14.0 trillion.
Friday rattled investors, the S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,659.44, the Dow slid 0.3% to 52,002.41 and the technology-packed Nasdaq Composite tumbled 2.1% to 26,140.03. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq logged their worst week since June, led by chip stock. The Dow and Nasdaq remain up 8.2% and 12.5% this year.
The Dow fell 3.81% on Oct. 14, 2.39% on Oct. 15 and 4.6% on Oct. 16. On Oct. 19, it opened at 2,246.74 and closed at 1,738.74, a 508-point plunge. The S&P 500 sank 20.47%, the Wilshire 5000 dropped 18% and estimated worldwide losses reached $1.71 trillion. Systems struggled: 195 of 2,257 NYSE-listed stocks faced delays or halts, and 95 S&P 500 stocks opened late while futures opened on time.
Possible triggers included a House bill to curb tax benefits for mergers and leveraged buyouts and a higher-than-expected trade deficit released Oct. 14. Many saw stocks as overvalued, while trade and budget deficits, rising interest rates and a falling dollar added to concern. Portfolio insurance (computer-driven selling of index futures), index arbitrage through program trading, weekend mutual fund redemptions and early selling ahead of the expected Monday drop amplified the rout. The 1988 Brady Report found margin calls ran about ten times their average size and judged portfolio insurance a possible contributing factor rather than the initial trigger.
On Oct. 20, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said the Fed "affirmed today its readiness to serve as a source of liquidity." It injected $17 billion that day, and the federal funds rate fell about half a percentage point. The S&P 500 bottomed at 230.30 in November 1987, down 31.6% from its Aug. 25 high of 336.77, and regained that high on July 26, 1989.
The NYSE adopted trading curbs in 1988, and regulators later created market-wide circuit breakers, used during the 2020 crash. Under the SEC's investor guidance , a single-day S&P 500 decline of 7% or 13% from the prior close before 3:25 p.m. ET halts trading for 15 minutes, with no halt at or after 3:25 p.m. A 20% decline at any time halts trading for the rest of the day. On Friday's close, those levels sit near 7,123, 6,664 and 6,128, so a 1987-size drop would breach the third. Losses can still pile up until each level is hit.
Michael Burry, whose bearish calls we have examined before , wrote in a Substack post, "I continue to believe it is possible the markets are near a major top." He pointed to leverage built by volatility-targeting and momentum strategies in a low-volatility market and compared it with the lead-up to Oct. 19, 1987. He is bearish on AI-linked stocks and reportedly holds short positions including NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) and Micron Technology ( NASDAQ:MU ), though he has warned short selling is high-risk.
According to Bloomberg on Oct. 9, Joachim Klement of Panmure Liberum says the AI bubble will burst in 2027 or 2028, with his target implying 36% downside for the S&P 500 by the end of 2027. He is the most bearish of eight strategists Bloomberg tracks; the other seven average about 14% upside. He does not recommend selling now.
The IMF's Global Financial Stability Report on Oct. 13 warned a sharp correction in AI stocks could spread through global markets, citing elevated AI valuations, higher government borrowing costs and a major cyberattack as possible catalysts. "Resilience is not safety," said the IMF's Athanasios Vamvakidis. Temasek CIO Rohit Sipahimalani calls a reversal of the AI trade a key risk.
Fund manager Adrian Day says some conditions mirror 1987, including higher rates, dollar and deficit concerns and an AI sector many consider overvalued, though yields aren't yet high enough to pull large sums out of stocks. Jim Paulsen, on the Excess Returns podcast Oct. 15, highlighted complacency and a possible "fairly nasty correction," particularly in new-era stocks, without a recession or all-out bear market. Riding a mania is one thing; knowing when to leave is the harder half, and we covered both in a free bubble survivor's handbook .
Citigroup ( NYSE:C ) strategists say solid 2027 earnings can support further gains, and Jefferies ( NYSE:JEF ) projects the S&P 500 could reach 9,000 by the end of 2027, per Invezz. The market has historically survived its worst days.
Watch third-quarter earnings and AI capital spending for signs the AI trade is strengthening or weakening.

His coverage centers on technology stocks and the broader macroeconomic trends, from interest rates to geopolitics,  that shape where markets are headed next. “The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. B ut the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15 ,” the investment bank said.

Worth remembering that French authorities have not linked the riots to immigrants.

The incident had sparked fears as it took place at the same airport where an attack with an explosives-laden drone happened in August, an incident German authorities attributed to Russia .

Curiously, the far-right National Rally party will not be represented neither by its presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, nor its prime ministerial candidate, Jordan Bardella, but a more junior figure, media reported.
In the meantime, Paris prosecutor said at least 145 people were still in custody following “various acts of vandalism, looting and attacks on law enforcement,” as reported by Le Figaro.
A person wears a mask near burning bicycles during civil unrest, the day after a national day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris, France. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters in Rome
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni will hold a crisis meeting with top security officials on Monday after two days of ransacking and looting in Milan allegedly perpetrated by gangs of hooded youths.
The unrest began on Saturday on the fringes of a protest against the rising cost of living. There were also clashes between police and protesters in Turin and Bologna.
Clashes in Bologna last weekend. Photograph: Alessandro Ruggeri/LaPresse/Shutterstock In Milan, more than 200 were detained by police, allegedly responsible for ransacking shops and smashing windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s Duomo. According to reports in the Italian press on Monday, 80% were minors, with many responding to appointments made on social media and sharing selfies as they bragged about the damage caused.
They were not believed to have been affiliated with any political party or organised groups or movements.
Meloni said on Saturday that the perpetrators were “thugs who exploit demonstrations to spread chaos, attack those who guarantee security, and hold entire cities to hostage”.
“To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not,” she wrote on X.
Police patrol streets after clashes with youth protesters near Piazza del Duomo in Milan, Italy. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock During her more than four years in power, Meloni has enacted tough security measures, including against peaceful protesters.
In July, her cabinet approved so-called “anti-maranza” legislation in response to a rise in child gangs and youth delinquency in city centres. “Maranza” is a slang term used to describe gangs of delinquent youths, usually coming from suburban areas.
Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.
There are no signs of French protests stopping anytime soon: the yellow vest movement, de gilets jaunes , has just announced a “second act” of protests for upcoming Saturday, 24 October – and then again a week after that, too.
The idea is to “keep the momentum going” until another major demonstration planned for 5 November, a group member told AFP.
A car burns near a graffiti reading "introduction to civil war" as clashes erupted during a demonstration against the "high cost of living", in Paris last weekend. Photograph: Guillaume Saligot/AFP/Getty Images Protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre museum in Paris in support of a nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”, the museum’s management and unions told AFP.
The museum could not open as scheduled because of a protest led by students from the Ecole du Louvre, management said. A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”
Protesters and students from art and culture schools block the entrance to the Louvre in Paris, France. Photograph: Abdul Saboor/Reuters Back to France , the authorities in Marseille have just issued a ban of any public gatherings and demonstrations “throughout the entire commune” from midday to 8pm.
Violent clashes and damage occurred before the start of a protest on the Canebiere and at the Old Port against the high cost of living in Marseille, France. Photograph: Alain ROBERT/SIPA/Shutterstock Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has responded to the latest wave of Russian attacks on Ukraine, confirming Ukraine had no prior warning from the US and seemingly accusing Washington of being in the state of denial about the reality of the war.
A woman stands next to a damaged beauty store near a metro station, which was hit by an overnight Russian missile strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters “Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners, ” he said.
“They again targeted energy facilities and infrastructure, but a medical clinic, a school, a metro station, and ordinary residential buildings were also damaged.”
Showing growing frustration with the attacks and continued criticism from US president Donald Trump , he said:
“ Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end. We have responded positively to EVERY ceasefire proposal. Russia’s response, time and again, has been ballistic missiles, “shaheds,” and killings.
Putin not only doesn’t want to end this war – he doesn’t even want to take any steps toward de-escalation. EVERY ONE of our partners has experienced this firsthand when they heard Russia’s refusals.
And it is crucial to call things what they are. To call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine defend lives. When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine’s air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners.
The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia’s desire to drag this war out.”
Italian police also clashed with protesters who threw stones and looted shops in Milan on Sunday during demonstrations over the rising cost of living, as lorry drivers blocked roads across southern Italy in protest at soaring fuel prices linked to the war in Iran.
Demonstrators light flares during an anti-government protest organised by the Italia in Piazza movement, at Piazza Duomo in Milan. Photograph: Piero Cruciatti/AFP/Getty Images Footage showed police in riot gear firing teargas and using water cannon after several hundred hooded protesters smashed shop windows and set bins alight in the area around Piazza del Duomo in central Milan.
Second day of the demonstration "Italia in piazza" against the high cost of living in Milan, Italy. Photograph: Nicola Marfisi/AGF/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen
Second day of the demonstration “Italia in piazza” against the high cost of living in Milan, Italy. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock The clashes echoed scenes of violence in neighbouring France , where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.
Meanwhile, lorry drivers have caused widespread disruption across southern Italy, blocking major roads and creating huge traffic jams in Sicily, Puglia and Calabria in protest at the mounting financial pressure on the haulage industry.
A handwritten sign reading ''Tutto esaurito'' (All sold out) covers the diesel and petrol price board at a self-service petrol station in Barletta, Italy. Photograph: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Hundreds of petrol stations have run out of fuel, while supermarkets are beginning to report shortages of several products, particularly fresh food. Pharmacies have also been affected, raising concerns about disruption to essential supplies.
“We are asking the government to urgently convene a meeting with industry associations. Otherwise, we will consider a nationwide strike,” said Pasquale Russo, president of Conftrasporto, an association representing Italian haulage companies.
“The situation is very concerning because the excessive price increases affecting the haulage industry have created a highly tense situation among transport companies, leading to spontaneous protests in some areas of the country,” he added.
In several parts of southern Italy, petrol stations have run out of both petrol and diesel, with motorists facing long queues at the few filling stations still operating. The road blockades have also caused extensive traffic disruption, with fears growing that prolonged protests could further disrupt supplies of food, fuel and other essential goods.
Fuel pumps are cordoned off with red and white barrier tape at a Q8 Easy self-service station in Barletta, Italy. Photograph: Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto/Shutterstock French president Emmanuel Macron has declined interior minister Laurent Nuñez’s offer to resign after widespread riots over the weekend, despite “failures in anticipation and intelligence” that were deemed to worsen the crisis engulfing the country.
Macron said Nuñez should stay to ‌ensure a chain of command is retained within the police and security forces, and has also asked Nuñez to set up ‌as quickly as possible new approaches to deal with looters, ​the Élysée Palace added, quoted by Reuters.
Macron has asked the minister to “put in place new operational methods for security forces” to get a grip over the crisis.
Saturday, one of the most violent days of unrest in years, left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country .
In a TV interview on Monday, Nuñez admitted that the police “lost control” in some cities during the protests.
Riots in central Paris over the weekend, with 2,400 people arrested nationally. Photograph: Poitout Florian/ABACA/Shutterstock In an address to the nation last night, Macron criticised “unbridled violence”.
Emmanuel Macron condemns violence in televised address – video
“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves how could French people do this to France ? ” he said.
Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after days of unrest and 2,400 arrests across France
Separately, I will also be keeping an eye on Ukraine , after another night of heavy attacks by Russia killing at least one and injuring eight people, and with conflicting reports about whether Kyiv authorities had been warned about the strikes.
A police officer inspects the site of a fitness club building hit by a Russian missile strike, amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters We should also get an update from Sweden , as the parliament’s speaker is set to decide on the next step in the government formation process there.
It’s Monday, 19 October 2026 , it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live .

Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the 1st time since 2023
Trump criticized the moving, calling on the Fed to "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES."
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Wednesday in an effort to battle back a monthslong surge of inflation set off by the Iran war . The move marks the central bank's first rate increase since July 2023.
The central bank hiked its benchmark rate a quarter of a percentage point, putting interest rates at a level between 3.75% and 4%.
Hours after the announcement, President Donald Trump criticized the move, repeating a call for lower interest rates that he has made on multiple occasions since his return to office last year.
The Federal Reserve Building is the headquarters of the Federal Reserve System and 12 Federal Reserve Banks, in Washington, D.C.
"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" Trump said in a social media post.
However later, Trump told ABC News that despite the Fed doing the opposite of what he has demanded he still has confidence in Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
"I’m relying on Kevin, but he’s got a very tough board," Trump said from the tarmac while traveling to a campaign rally in North Carolina, referring to the 12-member policymaking board. "He's got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high, they’re not appropriate."
Trump insisted the Fed raised rates “only for political reasons” and to hurt him.
“They’re raising the rates to make Trump do as bad as he can possibly do," he said. "The problem they have is that we have the greatest economy in history."
Earlier Wednesday, the board, including Trump-appointed Warsh, voted unanimously in favor of the rate increase.
That current level of interest rates marks a significant drop from a recent peak attained in 2023, but borrowing costs remain well above a 0% rate established at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Iran live updates: Sticker shock woes rise after Saudi refinery stops crude loading
The major stock indexes turned lower after the policy announcement. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 630 points, or 1.2%, while the S & P 500 dropped 0.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq ticked down 0.01%.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," Warsh said at a press conference in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. "The committee’s unanimous vote shows our resolve to achieve price stability on a timelier basis."
The move appears aimed at containing a recent bout of price increases. Global oil prices are hovering near a four-month high and the average price for a gallon of gasoline tops $4.30, according to AAA .
The U.S. economy has shown signs of additional strain in recent days, including a bond selloff that is pushing up borrowing costs for credit cards and mortgages.
The price woes previously divided central bankers eager to contain inflation but reluctant to cool off the economy and weaken the labor market.
The Fed opted to hold interest rates steady at its most recent meeting in July. Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board, however, voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction in a decade.

Iran updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs'
Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say
Warsh, who took the helm of the central bank in May, has vowed to cool off persistently elevated price increases.
"The Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices," Warsh said in remarks last month at the Fed's annual summer gathering in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference following Federal Open Market Committee meetings at Federal Reserve Headquarters, September 16, 2026 in Washington.
Prices rose 3.4% in August compared to a year earlier, maintaining the same level from the prior month, federal government data last week showed.
Inflation stands more than a percentage point higher than the Federal Reserve's target rate of 2%.
Despite a stubborn bout of inflation, the economy remains fairly robust by some measures.
A blockbuster jobs report earlier this month showed employers added 162,000 workers in August, demonstrating continued resilience for the nation's labor market. The economy grew over three months ending in June, defying fear of a downturn triggered by the Iran war.
Fighting in the Middle East kept global crude prices above $105 a barrel as of Wednesday, which amounted to a rise of about 50% since the Iran war broke out in late February.
Inflation holds steady at elevated level as Iran war pushes up gas prices
The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. stands at $4.36, putting it more than $1.30 higher than before the war, AAA data showed.
Record-high diesel prices have raised transport costs for many everyday products, including groceries, clothes and furniture.
The war in Iran, which began with a large-scale U.S.-Israeli attack in the winter, prompted Iran's near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which facilitates one-fifth of global crude supply. Saudi Arabia over the weekend shut down a key pipeline bypassing the strait, which further constrained oil delivery and put upward pressure on prices.
ABC News' Karen Travers, Michelle Stoddart and Devin Garbitt contributed to this report.

items.title: On Iran, Israel’s opposition is even more hawkish than Netanyahu
items.summary: In rest of the world, the Israeli PM is often blamed for the Iran war. His opponents say he hasn't been tough enough.
items.content:
Share On Iran, Israel’s opposition is even more hawkish than Netanyahu on social media
From left, Israeli opposition leaders Yair Lapid, Naftali Bennett, Gadi Eisenkot, Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan [Getty Images]
When Israel launched a sweeping military assault on Iran with the United States in February, the Israeli government enjoyed overwhelming support from the Jewish Israeli public.
Opposition parties lent their support to the army and backed the audacious step. Enmity towards the government in Iran is an issue mainstream Zionist parties agree on.

list 2 of 3 GCC condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as Yemen fighting intensifies
list 3 of 3 Hezbollah funding plan indicates a new challenge to Lebanon’s government
Then in June, Israel’s role in the confrontation halted abruptly with an announcement from US President Donald Trump, who said Iran and Israel had agreed to stop attacking each other.
That announcement – and Netanyahu’s decision to abide by it at the time – were unpopular in Israel. According to the Israel Democracy Institute , 65 to 70 percent of Jewish Israelis believe that stopping the war did not serve Israel’s national security interests.
As Israelis prepare to vote in national elections on October 27, Iran remains an important election issue for many. Opposition parties present Iran as an example of what they say are Netanyahu’s many failures. They promise to reset security and foreign policy if they’re elected.
The frontrunner, Gadi Eisenkot, says the conflict is unfinished. While saying that a change in Iran’s government was an unrealistic goal, Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of doing little to dismantle Iran’s nuclear programme. In September at the inauguration of his new party, Yashar, Eisenkot told supporters: “Ultimately, it must end in the destruction or dismantling of the Iranian nuclear programme, a goal not yet achieved with 440kg [970lb] of highly enriched uranium already there, which could quickly be turned into several nuclear devices.”
Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, who is now the head of the opposition in the Knesset, accuses Netanyahu of a strategic failure. He recently told the Atlantic Council that toppling the administration in Tehran is a realistic objective that requires a military escalation: “What Israel should do or the alliance should do is bomb all the energy facilities, especially on Kharg Island, but other places as well in order to make sure that the Iranian economy is demolished. And the reason is that it’s the only thing that will overturn the regime.”
Bombing this civilian infrastructure was actually something Netanyahu had lobbied for himself. An international outcry about such bombings likely constituting war crimes and Trump’s refusal to offer backing put the brakes on the plan.
Naftali Bennett, another former prime minister, says Israel must ensure its military dominance over the entire region. For Bennett, toppling the government in Iran and crushing it is a must. But he says that is not enough. The right-wing politician calls Qatar an “enemy” and says Turkiye is “the new Iran”, going as far as saying that military confrontation with the NATO member was inevitable.
“We will build an alliance of moderate forces in the region against the Islamist forces, against Iran, against Qatar, Turkiye and all the radical forces. We will take proactive actions to shape the region,” Bennett recently told supporters.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders do not rule out renewed confrontations. They focus on their confidence in the military and security establishment in assessing the dangers and dealing with them appropriately.
But opposition leaders have voiced concern that Netanyahu might resort to military escalation before the elections to tilt the balance in his favour or even disrupt them altogether – even though the prime minister said last week that he did not plan to attack Iran before the vote.
Those fears were elevated after Netanyahu posted a video from the Tel Nof Airbase warning that Israel’s enemies might attack before the elections. Other news reports said Netanyahu has shared intelligence on new threats from Iran with the US president.
Netanyahu was quickly rebuked by opposition leaders, who accused him of “political fearmongering”.
Lapid openly questioned Netanyahu’s motives. Lapid also accused him of using the Israeli military and bases as “backdrops” for election campaign videos.
Ultimately, most Israeli opposition parties and leaders aren’t opposed to war with Iran, and many are in fact even more hawkish in their approach towards Tehran than Netanyahu. They just don’t want a new military escalation before the elections.

Share Russia’s Lavrov discusses US war and regional security during Tehran visit on social media
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov (R) meets with Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi (Back), in Tehran on October 19, 2026 [AFP]
Tehran, Iran – Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran, to discuss the war with the United States and efforts to end it.
Lavrov landed in the Iranian capital on Monday afternoon on his first visit to Iran since February 2025.  Araghchi said talks with Lavrov had focused on regional developments, including the US-Israeli war on Iran.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says
list 3 of 3 Trump defends Russian sanctions relief, lashes out at Zelenskyy
“Regarding the Gulf and West Asia, we have had talks, and also on Ukraine and the Iranian-American negotiations,” Araghchi said in a press briefing.
He also called out Israel’s “dangerous expansion” in the region, which he blamed for the current hostilities.
“The lack of security in the Gulf and in the Strait of Hormuz … this is due to the Israeli-American aggression,” he said.
Lavrov said Russia is committed to a 20-year strategic partnership agreement with Iran, which officially came into force on October 2, 2026.
He is scheduled to hold talks with President Masoud Pezeshkian later on Monday.
Moscow said the trip was part of efforts to ease months of tension, since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran on February 28.
On Sunday, Lavrov was in Bahrain, which was heavily targeted by Iran during the war, to participate in a strategic dialogue session between Russia and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).
He was urged by GCC members to use Moscow’s influence with Tehran to press for “serious dialogue” and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been severely disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels.
GCC chief Jasem Al-Budaiwi said member states had faced more than 7,000 Iranian missiles and drones since the start of the war.
In the council’s closing statement, the six Arab countries said they wanted Iran’s nuclear and missile programmes, as well as its support for regional armed groups, to be included in future talks to end the war.
Nikita Smagin, an analyst and researcher on Iran and Russia’s role in the Middle East, said Lavrov’s trip reflects Moscow’s efforts to maintain working relations with all countries in the region.
He said Lavrov also wants to maintain Russia’s status as a mediator, despite the impact of the Ukraine war on its global reputation.
“The timing of visits to the Gulf monarchies and Iran, taking place almost simultaneously, is a deliberate signal: Moscow wants to show that it approaches relations with all these countries on broadly equal terms and is equally interested in cooperation with each of them,” Smagin said.
Lavrov told GCC ministers in Manama that the region was once again teetering on the brink of a full-scale war and Russia wanted to establish a regional architecture for “collective security”.
He said this could include combining initiatives from countries in the region, along with those put forward by Russia and China, with the aim of restoring maritime traffic and achieving lasting peace. The Russian foreign minister urged other regional states such as Iraq and Jordan, which have also been hit by Iranian strikes, to participate.
Lavrov expressed support for the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between Iran and the US in June, which later collapsed, as a framework for reducing tension.
Iran has said it wants a return to that agreement, and for Washington to honour a finalised bilateral deal between Iran and Oman to manage territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. This has been opposed by the US, which has established its own route in the waterway for shipping.
Intelligence reports cited by US media said that Russia and China are providing military support to Iran in the form of satellite imagery for targeting purposes and components for weapons.
But US President Donald Trump contradicted those reports last week, saying Moscow and Beijing would have “too much to lose” if they helped Iran.
Washington has also issued sanctions waivers for Russia in a bid to lower fuel prices driven up by the war against Iran.
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov (C) attends the 9th Joint Ministerial Meeting of the Strategic Dialogue between the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and the Russian Federation in Manama on October 18, 2026. [Fadhel Madan/AFP] Mixed intentions
Russia’s position on the Iran war is somewhat unusual, said Smagin. It has a partial interest in the conflict continuing, as higher oil prices and the severe restrictions on Iranian oil reaching China all benefit Moscow.
“Russia and Iran have been competing primarily for the Chinese market, so China is now effectively forced to buy Russian oil at higher prices because Iranian supplies are largely unavailable,” he said.
Smagin added that Russia does not want the conflict to escalate further, as the consequences could be unpredictable, but its leverage over either Iran or the US to influence the course of the conflict remains limited.
Russia will continue to expand relations with Tehran, Smagin said, including through Caspian Sea trade, and limited military cooperation with Iran.
“These efforts appear to be aimed less at generating economic returns than at expanding Russia’s political influence over Iran and the course of events,” he said.
Military strikes by Iran and the US to wrest control of the waterway have continued, with the US midterm elections approaching on November 3 .
In comments to the media, Trump threatened to “soon finish the job” with Iran, to which Iranian Foreign Minister Araghchi replied: “We have unfinished jobs too.”

Share Iran support for Houthis probed as Yemen war re-erupts and Saudi cities hit on social media
Houthi supporters rally in Sanaa, Yemen, while carrying Iranian flags and posters featuring former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei [File: Khaled Abdullah/Reuters]
New allegations about Iranian support for Yemen’s Houthis have emerged in media reports and official comments, highlighting the opaque nature of the alliance.
Media outlets have reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) aided the Houthis as they seized swaths of western Yemen and launched their most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia, which supports the internationally recognised Yemeni government fighting the Houthis.
Iranian support for the Houthis reported by the media includes training, intelligence, tactical guidance and help in targeting for drone and missile attacks.
If true, this will undoubtedly escalate tensions between Iran and Saudi Arabia, given that the kingdom has been targeted by dozens of Houthi drones and missiles in recent weeks, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people. Saudi energy facilities and oil tankers have also been targeted by the group.
Iranian backing, according to the reports, contributed to a September offensive by the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God). Those battles saw the Houthis win control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Iranian Mahan Air flights ferried IRGC paramilitary officers, drone parts, missile guidance systems and impact detonators to the Houthis in Yemen. IRGC officers were also reportedly on the front lines directing Houthi attacks.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, confirmed the presence of an external state actor behind the Houthis’ evolving arsenal but did not mention the state in question.
Al-Maliki noted that the Houthis, who have been at war with the government since 2014, have acquired advanced technologies with regional assistance.
This support has made the Houthis the first nonstate armed group to deploy ballistic missiles, offensive and suicide drones, and explosive-laden, high-speed boats, he said, although other Iranian allies, such as Hezbollah and Iranian militias, also possess such weaponry.
While the Houthis have stressed their independence from Iran, the two groups are ideologically aligned. They have also been accused of collaborating closely on military matters, evident in the Houthis’ missile arsenal.
Yemenis protest in support of the Houthis in Sanaa while carrying placards that read, “God is great. Death to America. Death to Israel. Curse the Jews. Victory to Islam” [File: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP] Operational planning
Analysts who spoke to Al Jazeera all agreed that the “regional assistance” the Houthis are receiving points towards the IRGC although Iran and the Houthis denied this.
One indication of this is the bombing of Sanaa International Airport in July before an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation travelling from Tehran was due to land. The Yemeni government, which said its forces carried out the attack, accused “the Iranian aircraft” of violating Yemeni airspace.
“[Recent reports] confirm what is known to experts for years as the Revolutionary Guard and Hezbollah experts engaged in managing the operational planning of battles against the Yemeni government and neighbouring countries, including the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst, told Al Jazeera.
“For example, the killing of Hassan Irlu [the Iranian ambassador to Houthi-controlled Yemen from 2020 to 2021], in Yemen after the military campaign on Marib in 2021 is one of the important indicators, in addition to Mahan aviation flights that transported more experts ahead of the Houthis’ internal and external escalation during July of this year.”
Ali al-Dahab, a military and strategic security affairs expert, agreed that the advanced weaponry used by the Houthis indicates an Iranian role in recent operations.
“What was leaked about Iranian support for the Houthis through this report did not add anything new except that it confirmed the confirmed, and what it added perhaps is that weapons smuggling, especially precision technologies for missiles and unmanned aircraft, takes place via small submarines,” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera.
“This issue is not everything being smuggled from Iran to the Houthis because there are interceptions of smuggled shipments revealed by the joint forces that were controlling the Mocha coast to Bab al-Mandeb before the Houthis’ control and before its break in September.”
Al-Dahab pointed out that while smugglers historically have used dhows, traditional wooden sailboats, to mislead naval coalitions, employing submarines is a new method used by the Houthis, akin to the tactics used by organised criminal groups in the Americas.
“It indicates that Iran focuses on the Houthis as the centre of military and security gravity south of the Red Sea and, therefore, provides them with these weapons, ammunition, expertise and information in anticipation of a battle that may break out in the Strait of Hormuz,” al-Dahab said. “Therefore, the Houthis play a supporting role for them in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.”
He warned of broader implications for international shipping with the Houthis now in control of Bab al-Mandeb, a narrow waterway linking the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea.
“The greatest danger now is that substate entities in the southern Red Sea and Gulf of Aden region unite under Iran’s leadership to confront the United States, Britain and Europe in general if a battle breaks out in the Gulf of Aden and the strait,” al-Dahab said.
Saudi Arabia and Iran had appeared to have patched up years of hostilities, including the suspension of diplomatic relations, with a China-brokered reconciliation agreement signed in Beijing in 2023.
Hesham Alghannam, a Riyadh-based fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said he doubts whether Saudi Arabia ever read the Beijing agreement as reconciliation but as a way of lowering tensions. Differences on geopolitical issues have continued between the two countries since the agreement was signed, including on Yemen, which lies on Saudi Arabia’s southern border.
“That isn’t a breach you can take to a lawyer. It’s keeping two files apart, and it works until someone says it out loud. That’s what’s changed,” Alghannam told Al Jazeera.
“Honestly, the deeper question was never whether Tehran signs [the agreement with Saudi Arabia]. It’s whether anything Tehran signs reaches the people holding the launchers,” he added, referring to Iran-aligned armed groups, such as the Houthis.
“We know how the other sequence ends. In 2014, the [Houthis] were offered seats, special status for Saada [the northern Yemeni stronghold of the Houthis] and a share of the executive authority in Yemen in return for handing the heavy weapons to the state,” he added.
What followed was the Houthis seizure of the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south, and the later killing of former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
“What followed was the seizure of the institutions, the president detained, parliament dissolved. The gains were banked, and the guns were kept,” Alghannam added.
“Saleh partnered with them, and he was killed in the street in 2017. Even after taking Sanaa, they didn’t become the state. They built a network of supervisors sitting over every official post. So the Saudi red line is one thing, no armed group or second army inside one state.”
The Saudi-led intervention in Yemen began in March 2015 and led to another direct conflict between Riyadh and the Houthis. Despite the massive support Saudi Arabia provided the internationally recognised government, it failed to retake Sanaa. This highlighted weaknesses within the anti-Houthi coalition, including divisions between the internationally recognised government and southern separatists.
“The lesson of 2015 wasn’t that acting firmly leads to a long war. It was that announcing a goal earlier than you should [do] does because once it’s said out loud, you’re bound to it long before you can deliver it,” he said.
“What Riyadh is trying to do now is easy to say and hard to do, but it’s crucial: tie the money and the weapons to real integration under one command, not to declared loyalty.”
A Yemeni family uses a shop in Taiz province in southwestern Yemen as a temporary shelter on October 8, 2026, after being displaced by renewed fighting between government forces and the Houthis [AFP] Strategic independence
Hassan Ahmadian, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Tehran, told Al Jazeera that Iran seeks technological independence for partners rather than perpetual reliance.
“This pattern is not like the United States pattern, which keeps whoever follows and allies with it in need of it, meaning [they have] to buy from the United States the weapons he needs, and the main weapon is basically not given to him if it is an Arab or Islamic country specifically,” he said.
“As for Iran, the ally is provided with the technology to create and produce the weapon, and this is not only in Yemen but in other regions and even in Gaza as much as possible where the technology was transferred because the view is different.”
Ahmadian said enabling Iran’s allies to produce their own weapons is a strategic move by Tehran and the Houthis are also motivated by breaking the Saudi siege on territories it controls in Yemen.
“The view is that this technology helps in confronting a common enemy, and therefore, strengthening this capability independently of Iran is in itself a strategic interest for Iran,” Ahmadian said.
“Notice that there is an advance for Ansar Allah [the Houthis] linked to the justice of the cause as there is a siege imposed on the Yemenis affecting 70 percent to 80 percent of the society controlled by Ansar Allah and the Sanaa government. So this cause, breaking the siege, is a just cause. … The regional circumstance gave [the Houthis] a motive that this is the time to pressure Saudi Arabia to break the siege, and this is what actually happened.”
